claims.text: Dynamic loading in a BCC high-entropy alloy induces a transient enhancement of short-range atomic order.
Enhanced short-range order creates dynamic obstacles to dislocation motion.
The dynamic obstacles increase strain hardening.
The dynamic obstacles increase yield strength.
The proposed mechanism maintains ductility despite increasing strength and hardening.
Near-equiatomic MoNbTaW is an example of a BCC high-entropy alloy suitable for the proposed test.
The initial BCC high-entropy alloy has a baseline level of short-range order.
Testing well below the order-disorder transition prevents thermal ordering effects.
Moderate to high strain rates can provoke dynamic atomic rearrangements in the alloy.
Dynamic local atomic rearrangements temporarily enhance short-range order.
Short-range-order fluctuations increase strain-rate sensitivity by impeding dislocation motion.
Heterogeneous deformation accommodates ductility under the proposed mechanism.
Relative to a chemically simpler BCC baseline alloy, the high-entropy alloy will exhibit greater transient short-range-order evolution during dynamic loading.
Transient short-range-order evolution will be observable as diffraction-peak shifts or broadening.
Relative to the baseline, the high-entropy alloy will have greater strain-rate sensitivity during dynamic loading.
Relative to the baseline, the high-entropy alloy will have greater yield strength during dynamic loading.
Relative to the baseline, the high-entropy alloy will have a greater work-hardening rate during dynamic loading.
A chemically simpler near-equiatomic BCC baseline alloy will show minimal or no transient short-range-order evolution under identical conditions.
The mechanism may cease to operate when the loading timescale is too short for short-range-order rearrangement.
The mechanism may not apply when thermal effects dominate.
